content: Rhubarb is a perennial plant that grows from thick, short rhizomes and belongs to the genus Rheum within the family Polygonaceae. This family also includes plants such as dock, sorrel, knotweeds, knotgrasses, and buckwheat. The plant features large, somewhat triangular leaf blades that are supported by long, fleshy petioles. Its flowers are small, greenish-white, and grow in large, compound leafy inflorescences. Although rhubarb is botanically classified as an herb, it is often used in culinary applications as if it were a fruit. In the United States, rhubarb was considered a vegetable until the 1940s, when customs officials reclassified it as a fruit based on its culinary use. The plant is native to Asia and is believed to have been used historically by Mongolian tribes, particularly the Tatars of the Gobi region. Rhubarb has also grown wild along the banks of the Volga River for centuries, possibly introduced by Eurasian tribes such as the Scythians, Huns, Magyars, or Mongols. While rhubarb has a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine, its use as a food product is relatively recent, first documented in 17th-century England after sugar became more affordable for the general population. Today, rhubarb is cultivated in many regions, primarily for its fleshy petioles, commonly referred to as rhubarb sticks or stalks. In temperate climates, rhubarb is one of the earliest food plants available for harvest, typically in mid to late spring (April/May in the Northern Hemisphere and October/November in the Southern Hemisphere). The petioles can be prepared in various ways, often stewed to produce a tart sauce that is sweetened with sugar and used as a filling for pies, tarts, and crumbles. This common culinary application has earned rhubarb the nickname pie plant. In Germany, the term Rhabarber is used, but the slang term pie plant is also recognized. Rhubarb is often cooked with strawberries to create jams and can even be used to make wine or as an ingredient in cakes. Historically, in parts of the United Kingdom and Sweden, children would enjoy a simple treat of a tender rhubarb stick dipped in sugar. In the UK, the first rhubarb of the year is traditionally grown in dark sheds under candlelight in the Rhubarb Triangle of Wakefield, Leeds, and Morley. In warmer climates, rhubarb can grow year-round, but in colder regions, the above-ground parts of the plant die back in winter and regrow from the root in early spring. Rhubarb can also be forced to grow earlier by raising the local temperature, often achieved by placing an upturned bucket over the emerging shoots. Medicinally, rhubarb has been used as a strong laxative and for its astringent effects on the mucous membranes of the mouth and nasal cavity. There are approximately 60 extant species of rhubarb. The most commonly used species in cooking are Rheum rhabarbarum (Garden Rhubarb) and Rheum rhaponticum (commonly called False Rhubarb, despite being a true rhubarb). Cultivated varieties grown for consumption are generally recognized as Rheum × hybridum by the Royal Horticultural Society. The medicinal drug rheum is derived from the rhizomes and roots of Rheum officinale (Medicinal Rhubarb), which is also native to Asia, as is Rheum palmatum (Turkey Rhubarb). Another species, Rheum nobile (Sikkim Rhubarb), is native to the Himalayas. Additionally, rhubarb species serve as larval food plants for various Lepidoptera species, including the Brown-tail, Buff Ermine, Cabbage Moth, Large Yellow Underwing, The Nutmeg, Setaceous Hebrew Character, and Turnip Moth. Rhubarb leaves are toxic due to their high content of oxalic acid, a corrosive and nephrotoxic compound found in many plants. The estimated median lethal dose (LD50) of pure oxalic acid is approximately 375 mg/kg of body weight, which equates to about 25 grams for a 65 kg (140 lb) individual. While the oxalic acid content in rhubarb leaves varies, a typical concentration is around 0.5%. This means that consuming approximately five kilograms of rhubarb leaves would be required to reach a lethal dose, which is highly unlikely due to their extreme sourness. However, rhubarb leaves are also believed to contain an additional, unidentified toxin. The petioles, in contrast, contain much lower levels of oxalic acid, particularly when harvested before mid-June in the Northern Hemisphere. Nevertheless, consuming the petioles can still cause a slightly rough sensation on the teeth. The roots and stems of rhubarb are rich in anthraquinones, such as emodin and rhein, which have cathartic and laxative properties. These compounds are yellow or orange in color and may cause discoloration of the urine. Rhubarb has occasionally been misused as a slimming agent due to its laxative effects. The word rhubarb has also been used in various non-botanical contexts. In acting, extras in a crowd scene would often repeat the word rhubarb to simulate the sound of general background chatter. This practice led to the term being used to describe superfluous or irrelevant text in speech or writing. In American English, the equivalent term is walla. Additionally, rhubarb has been used to describe a loud argument or fight, particularly in baseball, where it refers to a bench-clearing brawl. In the 1989 film Batman, the Joker uses the phrase never rub another man's rhubarb as a warning to Bruce Wayne. The phrase out in the rhubarb patch is sometimes used to describe a remote or neglected area, as rhubarb is often grown at the edges of gardens. The term Donkey Rhubarb is a colloquial reference to Japanese knotweed and is sometimes used as slang for cannabis in parts of Canada. Rhubarb is also frequently mentioned in the radio program A Prairie Home Companion, particularly in the form of the fictitious product Be-Bop-A-Re-Bop Rhubarb Pie.
